  • Repository discovery proposes lessons about recurring work in the repository.

Each maintenance specialist keeps, adapts, retires or defers every lesson in its scope. Large manifests are processed in complete batches bounded by serialized context size; every batch requires exactly one decision per supplied ID. The host binds that ID to its frozen supplied revision and owns revision increments; agents do not manage version counters. Missing delivery evidence makes the specialists abstain. Missing or duplicate decisions fail that specialist's reconciliation instead of reporting success.

Maintenance also consolidates overlapping advice within the same repository or exact graph/node/ repository-qualified scope. It keeps or adapts one canonical card and retires redundant paraphrases, while still deciding every supplied ID/revision. Distinct causes and operations remain separate.

There is no findings count quota. Discovery returns every distinct lesson that qualifies; zero new lessons is valid. A lesson needs evidence of expensive failure or substantial exploration, a concrete recommendation and a reason to expect reuse. Task summaries, generic advice and facts obvious from nearby code do not qualify. Titles have at most 96 UTF-8 bytes; recommendations have at most 640. The store keeps evidence pointers and provenance separately from the injected card. Use stable paths and identifiers in advice. Admission detects common literal root-relative file:line pointers; semantic maintenance also checks other positional forms. Legacy cards remain readable; maintenance must adapt them to stable guidance or defer, rather than keep or merely renumber their source positions.

Discovery checks observed main-run cost before accepting a proposal. Two timeout/crash completions or two provably rejected review-loop visits can qualify. Repository discovery also accepts exploration with at least three distinct tool callbacks spanning five minutes. A single ordinary response-format correction does not qualify. Graph discovery requires the repeated-failure path. Review cost is counted by distinct rejected rounds within one map scope, attributed to the workers in that round's serial prefix. Supported layouts use a worker prefix followed by direct verifiers or all-join verifier groups; error-only choice wrappers require a proven branch. The scanner checks supported inner loops separately and skips enclosing nested loops or maps, incomplete/ambiguous rounds, seeded histories and unsupported guards. Error exits are false only when every recorded visit of that node has a settled non-error outcome; absent or unknown outcomes are not proof. Repository discoveries also need a current file citation and a matching file, folder or verified identifier association. These conservative checks establish cost; the specialist must still establish what was learned, why it recurs and whether current source supports it. Maintenance can update supplied lessons even when discovery has no eligible evidence. Rejected discovery proposals log the failed validation stage (including card field errors) without logging the proposed lesson text. Exploration proof must come from the cited hooks themselves, rather than uncited tools elsewhere in the run. Postmortem history is read in bounded pages; its fixed transcript budget reclaims old records from the execution consuming the most space, so a verbose late reviewer cannot displace all worker evidence. Reads stop between bounded pages on cancellation. Final context trimming shrinks the largest evidence array first and retains an excerpt per execution where the byte budget allows. Truncation remains explicit.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
These optional sections belong in the runtime JSON, alongside harness, provider, size and nodes. Both memory scopes and the postmortem default to enabled:

{
  "activeMemory": {
    "repository": true,
    "graph": true,
    "budgetBytes": 2048
  },
  "globalAgents": {
    "postmortem": {
      "enabled": true,
      "sourceNode": "worker",
      "timeoutMs": 120000
    }
  }
}

Set repository or graph to false to stop both retrieval and collection for that scope. Set both to false to disable Active Memory. Set postmortem.enabled to false to retain recall without collecting or maintaining lessons. These settings apply to each run, so saved profiles can keep different policies.

sourceNode must identify an agent binding in the authored graph. Omit it to inherit the first worker in graph order, then the first agent verifier. All four specialists inherit that node's exact model, effective harness/provider lane, effort and declared connections. They use separate sessions. Each scope's opt-out disables both its maintenance and discovery. A maintenance specialist cannot change the other scope even if its model returns a foreign ID. Only built-in global agents are accepted initially.

budgetBytes is a cumulative context budget per provider session, including card framing. It must be 1 through 16384; cards that do not fit remain undelivered. The postmortem's shared wall-clock budget is timeoutMs, from 1 through 600000. Provider startup, investigation and all maintenance batches consume that budget. An interrupted or failed maintenance pass never claims that the entire supplied manifest was reconciled.

docs.title: Indexing and retrieval
docs.text:
A run freezes an immutable, scoped snapshot. Matching uses resident inverted indexes and performs no model calls, network lookups or filesystem scans. Repository lessons can independently associate with multiple literal files, folders, identifiers or groups of keywords.

Match Score Exact root-relative file 1000 Containing folder 800 Exact whole identifier 700 All terms in an indexed keyword group 500

Each card gets its strongest independent match. Repeated words do not increase its score. Retrieval sorts by descending score, then lesson ID, and returns complete cards within the remaining budget. Impact determines admission, so retrieval ranks by relevance alone. An ID/revision is supplied once per provider session. A new session can receive it again.

An identifier is a literal name such as configure_bedrock or CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK. Matching preserves the whole name and also splits snake/camel names into topic words for keyword groups. Groups require two through four specific terms; individual broad words cannot retrieve a card. Matching is deterministic and uses exact terms in this version.

Native path fields take priority. Paths resolve against the tool's working directory and the workspace root, with component-aware folder matching. Shell arguments provide additional signals; simple cd folder && ... commands are recognized. An opaque script that never exposes its file paths can miss relevant cards. The matcher does not trace arbitrary program filesystem access.

Repository cards arrive through native harness hooks:

  • Codex and Claude use PreToolUse additional context through a small native callback helper.
  • Copilot uses its private RPC preToolUse callback.
  • Pi uses a product-owned extension that appends cards to the tool result, including in contained mode where automatic project extensions remain disabled.

Context guides subsequent model decisions. It cannot revise a tool call already issued, so reads and searches provide the most useful early triggers. Managed policy or disabled native hooks can prevent injection. Transport failures leave the task running; missing delivery evidence makes maintenance abstain. Hook receipts record returned context, not proof that the model followed it.

Graph lessons enter the node's instructions after admission validation. Their scope is the authored compiled graph hash plus node ID, optionally repository. Memory injection never changes that hash, the authored graph, permissions or output contracts. Authored graph changes create a new scope; this version does not transfer guidance across graph versions.

docs.title: Persistence and run completion
docs.text:
Local runs share one database across repositories, outside repository checkouts:

Platform Default database path Linux / macOS ~/.local/state/zeroshot/active-memory/lessons.sqlite3 Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\zeroshot\state\active-memory\lessons.sqlite3

On Unix, XDG_STATE_HOME selects $XDG_STATE_HOME/zeroshot/active-memory/lessons.sqlite3 when set. ZEROSHOT_STATE_DIR takes precedence on every platform and selects $ZEROSHOT_STATE_DIR/active-memory/lessons.sqlite3. Changing these variables selects another store; it does not move existing lessons.

Executable and skill updates preserve this directory, as does normal run and workspace cleanup. A direct target uses <target-storage>/active-memory/lessons.sqlite3; preserve its storage volume when recreating the Docker container.

Zeroshot does not create automatic backups. To back up or move memory, stop all Zeroshot processes using the store and copy the whole active-memory/ directory, including any SQLite journal files. Restore it while those processes are stopped. Deleting the state directory or losing the storage volume loses its lessons unless you have a backup.

The host owns the database outside the checkout and publishes all shared-store mutations. Workers receive a run-scoped retrieval capability. Reconciliation uses expected revisions, atomic transactions and deletion tombstones, so concurrent runs cannot silently overwrite a newer lesson or recreate a retired record from a stale snapshot. Newly published lessons become available to future runs.

Maintenance can replace lessons or retire obsolete ones. Previous contents are not archived, and there is no built-in undo; deletion tombstones retain IDs and revisions rather than card contents.

The main graph outcome is durably latched before postmortem. Ordinary postmortem failures appear in run logs and preserve that outcome. After a controller restart, confirmed runtime cleanup preserves the latched outcome and marks interrupted auxiliary token usage incomplete. Cancellation stops and drains the optional work; uncertain provider cleanup retains the runtime's existing failure handling. Global-agent work stays outside reducer execution history and checkpoint seeds, while its model usage contributes to run totals.

The native hook records bounded tool receipts in memory for postmortem evidence, including when a tool matches no card. Receipts contain the node, tool name, time and a few associated workspace paths; they exclude arguments and results and do not claim that a tool succeeded. The first and latest receipts survive a fixed 512-record cap. Hidden reasoning is not required or inspected.

Local and target stores do not synchronize automatically. Platform integration and ACP integration are outside this version. Embedders must explicitly select a host-owned memory namespace; the generic hosting configuration does not create an organization-wide store implicitly.

docs.title: Initialize from local history
docs.text:
Use the dedicated zeroshot-memory-init skill to initialize memory from all qualified local run history. It orchestrates separate discovery subagents for each selected run, then fresh graph and repository maintenance specialists against the recorded current checkouts.

zeroshot update installs or refreshes the skill; npm installation includes it too. If upgrading through an older updater that only knows the zeroshot skill, run zeroshot update again after the binary update. See skill installation for user-scope locations and conflict handling.

The skill uses one resumable command, independent of the invoking folder:

zeroshot memory init --directory /path/to/session
zeroshot memory init --directory /path/to/session --ignore-repos owner/repo,other-repo --ignore-graphs autoresearch,GRAPH_HASH

--ignore-repos and --ignore-graphs accept comma-separated, space-separated or repeated values. Matching is exact and case-sensitive. Repository values match aliases reported in the inventory: checkout folder name, absolute checkout path, admitted repository name, forge owner/repo, or the opaque repo:... namespace. A short folder name excludes every matching repository. Graph values match the exact authored root name or graph hash reported in the inventory; original profile names are not retained in historical admission. There is no --cwd flag.

The first call creates a private session outside repository checkouts and inventories finished local native runs across all repositories. Each run carries its own repository namespace, aliases, workspace, graph name and hash. Checkouts are resolved from recorded workspace metadata, with current remote identity checked against admitted sources. Admissions without a remote are matched against repository IDs independently resolved from the current checkout or its registered remote; folder names and historical display aliases cannot prove identity. A historical remote, when present, still requires its exact remote-derived identity. During inventory, unavailable or changed checkouts are explicit exclusions and do not prevent other repositories from proceeding. Nothing is cloned or fetched. Current checkout probes are shared across runs.

Subsequent calls return the next work through phase and next_action. The skill classifies every candidate, fills the exported specialist response files, and calls the same command to advance. Saved ignore lists apply on resume without repeating flags; conflicting lists require a new session. Discovery findings remain staged until every supplied card has a maintenance decision. The CLI validates the same impact rules and lesson contracts as after-run postmortems; it makes no model calls and uses no provider credentials. Host subagents use the host's model connections.

The newest selected run for each repository supplies its recorded current checkout for maintenance. Graph maintenance covers each exact graph and repository scope; unqualified graph cards shared by several repositories are reconciled once. Repository cards stay within their own repository. Specialist contexts never include another repository's cards. Every selected checkout is fingerprinted, and all mutations across repositories publish in one transaction after complete maintenance coverage. Remote and runtime namespace identities are rechecked before review and publication, including changes to Git configuration that leave tracked files unchanged. If a selected checkout disappears or changes identity after staging, publication stops; restore it or start a new session with appropriate exclusions. Supplied cards are never silently dropped. Citations through symlinks require their canonical targets to be tracked or nonignored too, so the cited bytes participate in the fingerprint.

phase: complete returns the publication receipt. Retrying a completed session returns that result without repeating mutations. Session locks prevent concurrent advancement, including interrupted history export. Atomic SQLite receipts recover a process interruption between publication and its local completion checkpoint; checkpoints use durable atomic file replacement before receipts are removed. Source or lesson changes preserve staged findings for fresh maintenance work; digest-bound task responses prevent stale reuse. Deferred discoveries remain inactive. There is no findings count quota.

Current source includes tracked and nonignored untracked files and executable permissions. Ignored artifacts cannot be maintenance authority. Keep code stable during final review and publication; the filesystem and database cannot share a transaction. The CLI does not pull or change branches. Historical exploration receipts were not persisted, so backfill cannot reconstruct them from elapsed time. Unreadable, unfinished, opted-out and unprovable-repository runs remain explicit exclusions. Old ledgers are read-only; initialization usage belongs to the host session. Platform and Docker target history are outside this workflow.

Inventory can prove an attached run's repository from a unique eligible remote even when its recorded checkout now has detached HEAD. Publication uses that checkout's current runtime namespace, reported per run. Existing local path namespaces do not migrate automatically when a checkout later acquires an admitted remote source.

docs.title: Observe and control runs
docs.text: Run state persists when an observation client leaves, and reconnecting does not change the run lifetime.

docs.title: Browser
docs.text:
Run zeroshot ui, then select a run in Runs. The read-only graph uses that run's admitted definition. Select a node for its inputs, outputs, decisions, and transcript; use the timeline to replay its history. Active runs update live. Seeking pauses following; Go live returns to the latest event. Scrolling a transcript keeps the graph live and follows new output only when you reach the bottom.

For a direct target, open /ui/ on its configured public origin. Closing either browser view leaves the run active.

docs.title: Foreground and detached submission
docs.text:
zeroshot run follows the durable event stream by default and writes NDJSON. Add --detach to return after submission:

zeroshot run \
  --title "Update parser" \
  --template software-change --delivery none \
  --input input.json \
  --uniform-runtime-config runtime.json \
  --detach

Ctrl-C closes the terminal stream and leaves the controller running.

docs.title: Inventory and current status
docs.text:
These commands are read-only and return JSON:

zeroshot list
zeroshot status RUN_ID

A run ID belongs to the controller or target that created it. Pass --target NAME when reading one from a named target.

docs.title: Resume event and log streams
docs.text:
watch follows status events; logs follows safe provider and controller log records. Both accept an opaque cursor and resume strictly after it:

zeroshot watch RUN_ID --after STATUS_CURSOR
zeroshot logs RUN_ID --after LOG_CURSOR

Cursors are opaque, so store the last fully consumed value and pass it back unchanged. logs --execution EXECUTION_REF restricts output to one execution selector from status.

The producer records each log timestamp as a positive JavaScript-safe Unix epoch millisecond, and durable replay preserves it.

docs.title: Attach to an active execution
docs.text:
Status can expose an active execution reference. Attach to its interactive event stream with:

zeroshot attach RUN_ID EXECUTION_REF

Closing the attachment stream does not cancel the execution.

docs.title: Restart or resume a failed run
docs.text:
Failed local runs and direct targets retain their workspace. Restart the original graph using its latest files with:

zeroshot resume RUN_ID

To resume at an earlier node, list its available input checkpoints and select one:

zeroshot checkpoints RUN_ID
zeroshot resume RUN_ID --from-checkpoint CHECKPOINT_ID

Add --target NAME to both commands for a named target. Checkpoint listings are paginated; use --after CHECKPOINT_ID with the returned nextAfter value to fetch the next page.

A selected checkpoint restores the files from immediately before its node and the completed prerequisite outputs. The selected node runs again. Parallel and mapped groups have one checkpoint for the whole outer group, including nested groups and all mapped batches; individual concurrent writers do not have separate snapshots. Read-only boundaries can share the same workspace bytes.

Both modes create a new run ID, keep the original graph, input, source, and delivery lineage, and resolve credentials again. The successor does not inherit provider sessions, secrets, or previous token usage. Selecting a checkpoint replaces later workspace edits, including untracked and ignored files. Restart restores the latest completed snapshot and starts the graph at its root. A sudden target loss can precede the next snapshot boundary, so the last writer may run again. Local workspaces must be idle while they are restored.

Local and Docker targets deduplicate checkpoints in a private Restic repository beside their run storage and advertise openengine.workspace-checkpoints/v1. They retain that repository only for a failed recovery lineage and delete it after a successful run. Platform exposes recovery through authenticated hosted run routes, so failed-run checkpoints remain available for 30 days after the original capsule is removed. Platform resolves declared connections from their original references. Direct-target resume reuses the original source connection authorization and resolves fresh values; export GH_TOKEN again when the run uses it for checkout or GitHub delivery.

docs.title: Stop only with explicit intent
docs.text:
force-stop is the destructive run-lifetime command:

zeroshot force-stop RUN_ID

The command asks the controller to stop active work and writes the resulting status as JSON. Read status first if another operator may already have stopped the run, or if it may have completed.

Python follows the same rule. A timeout or task cancellation detaches observation; await run.force_stop() changes the run lifetime.

docs.title: Python SDK
docs.text: the-open-engine-zeroshot is a typed asynchronous client for local, direct, and named hosted targets. Each platform wheel contains the corresponding Zeroshot executable, which keeps the client and engine on one release line.

docs.title: Install and run
docs.text:
Download the wheel for your OS and CPU from Python SDK releases. x86_64 wheels target Intel/AMD CPUs; arm64/aarch64 target ARM CPUs, including Apple silicon. Windows x64 uses win_amd64. Replace WHEEL_FILE with its local path:

python -m pip install WHEEL_FILE

import asyncio

from zeroshot import Client, UniformRuntime


async def main() -> None:
    runtime = UniformRuntime(
        harness="codex",
        provider="openai",
        model="PROVIDER_MODEL_ID",
        effort="high",
    )

    async with Client(runtime=runtime) as client:
        result = await client.run(
            "Add JSON status output and cover it with focused tests.",
            cwd="/path/to/folder",
            wait_timeout=21_600,
        )

    result.raise_for_failure()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Opening a client captures the current folder; the default preset is Preset("software-change"). An omitted delivery selector uses the native template default: a PR for software-change, a comment for pr-review and issue-review. PR publication requires a Git checkout, GitHub access, and the declared github.GH_TOKEN connection. Use Preset("software-change", delivery="none") for local changes without publication. Per-run cwd= paths resolve from that captured folder, or LocalTarget.workspace when supplied. Local graphs without Git delivery accept plain folders. Push needs committed Git and a remote; PR and merge need a supported forge (GitHub today). Choose the harness, provider, and model. run() submits once and waits; submit() returns a durable Run handle immediately.

docs.title: Watch a submitted run
docs.text:
from zeroshot import Client, UniformRuntime


async def observe(runtime: UniformRuntime) -> None:
    async with Client(runtime=runtime) as client:
        run = await client.submit("Update the parser.")
        status = await run.status()
        async for event in run.watch(after=status.cursor):
            print(event)

A RunWaitTimeout carries the still-active run handle, and cancelling the Python task detaches in the same way. Neither action stops native work; only await run.force_stop() changes run lifetime.

docs.title: Run on a direct target
docs.text:
Local execution uses LocalTarget. Docker/direct and hosted targets require a committed Git source, selected from the client workspace or per-run repository=, branch=, and revision=. repository= accepts a credential-free HTTPS/SSH Git URL or GitHub owner/name shorthand; source_connection= selects a named connection used only for Git checkout and delivery:

from zeroshot import Client, DirectTarget, UniformRuntime


async def run_direct(runtime: UniformRuntime) -> None:
    target = DirectTarget("http://127.0.0.1:8080")

    async with Client(target=target, runtime=runtime) as client:
        result = await client.run("Update the parser.")

    result.raise_for_failure()

docs.title: Submit a hosted merge plan
docs.text:
Log in with the CLI first, then pass that target's local name to HostedTarget. A plan uses one explicit repository and branch plus one hosted profile. The profile must contain exactly one current Git merge delivery node. Agent bindings must not declare GH_TOKEN; only the Git delivery binding may declare it.

from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta

from zeroshot import Client, HostedTarget, MergePlanRequest, MergePlanRun


async def submit_release_plan() -> None:
    request = MergePlanRequest(
        title="Release checkout update",
        repository="the-open-engine/zeroshot",
        branch="main",
        profile="org:software-change",
        expires_at=(datetime.now(UTC) + timedelta(days=1)).isoformat(),
        runs={
            "backend": MergePlanRun(input={"task": "Update the API."}),
            "frontend": MergePlanRun(input={"task": "Update the client."}),
            "integrate": MergePlanRun(
                input={"task": "Verify the combined changes and run the release tests."},
                needs=("backend", "frontend"),
            ),
        },
        submission_key="checkout-release-1",
    )

    async with Client(target=HostedTarget("platform")) as client:
        plan = await client.submit_plan(request)
        status = await plan.wait(wait_timeout=21_600)

    if not status.succeeded:
        raise RuntimeError(f"merge plan ended as {status.state}")

Submission is atomic, and every node receives a stable run ID. needs gates readiness only; plan nodes have no output interpolation or shared mutable input. After dependencies merge, Platform materializes the node against an exact source revision. When materialization completes, readyAt is set and the node's queue deadline is the earlier of plan expiry and seven days after readyAt. A merge conflict is repaired by the conflicting run itself in the same checkout and delivery loop. A descendant cannot repair a failed predecessor; it ends as dependency_failed. The v1 API has no aggregate event stream, so MergePlan.watch() polls and yields changed snapshots.

docs.title: Pass exact protocol documents
docs.text:
GraphSpec and RuntimePlan wrap exact JSON mappings without loss. Python neither copies the Rust schemas nor applies its own semantic checks:

from collections.abc import Mapping
from typing import Any

from zeroshot import Client, GraphSpec, RunRequest, RuntimePlan


async def submit_exact(
    client: Client,
    graph_document: Mapping[str, Any],
    runtime_document: Mapping[str, Any],
) -> None:
    request = RunRequest(
        title="Repair checkout",
        graph=GraphSpec.from_dict(graph_document),
        initial_input={"ticket": "OE-123"},
        runtime=RuntimePlan.from_dict(runtime_document),
        submission_key="oe-123-attempt-1",
    )

    result = await client.run(request)
    result.raise_for_failure()

An opaque RuntimePlan may carry per-node lanes and passes through unchanged, while UniformRuntime applies one lane to every agent node.

Before starting a local controller or contacting a direct target, the bundled executable performs the same preflight as the CLI.

The Python API reference documents the public client surface.

docs.title: Build a review loop
docs.text:
This guide builds a custom graph that sends one coding task through a worker and two independent reviewers. When either reviewer rejects the change, the loop runs the same worker again with both reviewers' feedback. The run succeeds when both accept, and fails after four passes.

The built-in software-change template already does this with more recovery paths. Build the loop yourself when you want to change the reviewers, their instructions, or the bounds.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
This guide assumes you have completed Run a first task: Zeroshot is installed, the Codex CLI is signed in, and you have a folder with an HTTP service to change.

The worker edits the selected folder

Back up work you want to protect, or commit or stash it in a Git checkout.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
The example has three files, plus an optional runtime plan for cross-vendor review. Download them or copy them from the sections below, and keep them outside the folder you are changing, for example in ~/review-loop/, so they stay out of the change.

File Purpose input.json The task review-loop.graph.json Worker, reviewers, loop, and terminal result review-loop.runtime.json Harness, provider, models, and session scopes review-loop.cross-vendor.runtime.json Optional: Codex worker, Claude Code reviewers

The graph controls order and data flow. The runtime plan binds only the three nodes that run agents.

The excerpts in steps 1 to 4 leave out fields; the complete graph is in step 5.

docs.title: 1. Define input and state
docs.text:
A graph starts with a profile, an initial input type, and a policy. The caller supplies only the task:

"initialInput": {
  "kind": "record",
  "fields": {
    "task": { "type": { "kind": "string" }, "required": true }
  }
}

The root seq declares a state record with task plus one feedback field per reviewer, acceptanceFeedback and codeFeedback. The root may add required fields that have an implicit empty value, so both feedback strings start as "" without appearing in input.json.

Every structural node (seq, loop, par, choice) declares its own state type, so the graph repeats this record. Input bindings copy state into an agent's input. Promoted state paths copy updated state from a group back to the group that encloses it.

docs.title: 2. Add the worker
docs.text:
The worker is a step. It reads the task and both feedback fields:

{
  "kind": "step",
  "name": "worker",
  "worker": "builtin.agent.software-worker@1",
  "instructions": "Implement the requested change. If reviewer feedback is present, address both diagnostics before returning. Work in the shared repository and run focused checks.",
  "output": { "kind": "null" },
  "writeBindings": [],
  "attempts": 1
}

The full node also declares an input record and three inputBindings, one per field. Its output is null because the worker changes files in the shared workspace rather than returning data.

The worker value is a label local to this graph. The builtin. names only mirror the built-in template; they add no behavior. Admission derives each worker's contract from the node's declared input, output, signals, and diagnostic, so a label used on several nodes must keep the same declaration and binding kind. Every agent node needs authored instructions.

docs.title: 3. Run two reviewers in parallel
docs.text:
A par group named reviews runs two verifiers against the same workspace. Each verifier returns a verdict signal and a diagnostic, and writes the diagnostic message into its feedback field:

{
  "kind": "verifier",
  "name": "acceptance",
  "worker": "builtin.agent.acceptance-verifier@1",
  "signals": { "verdict": ["accepted", "rejected"] },
  "writeBindings": [
    {
      "value": { "node": "acceptance", "channel": "diagnostic", "path": ["message"] },
      "target": ["acceptanceFeedback"]
    }
  ]
}

The code verifier has the same shape and writes codeFeedback. Zeroshot tells verifiers not to edit the material under review; that is an instruction, not a filesystem boundary.

The all join waits for both reviewers. reviews promotes both feedback paths into the iteration state, and the iteration promotes them into the loop state, so the next worker pass can read them.

docs.title: 4. Stop on two acceptances
docs.text:
The loop body is a seq of the worker and reviews. Loops are do-while: until is checked after each pass, so the worker always runs at least once.

"until": {
  "kind": "all",
  "guards": [
    {
      "kind": "in",
      "value": { "name": "acceptance", "source": "signal", "field": "verdict" },
      "labels": ["accepted"]
    },
    {
      "kind": "in",
      "value": { "name": "code", "source": "signal", "field": "verdict" },
      "labels": ["accepted"]
    }
  ]
},
"maxIterations": 4

A loop reports converged or exhausted through its terminated group control. A choice after the loop turns that control into an explicit terminal:

{
  "kind": "choice",
  "name": "loop_result",
  "branches": [
    {
      "when": {
        "kind": "in",
        "value": { "name": "review_loop", "source": "group", "field": "terminated" },
        "labels": ["converged"]
      },
      "node": { "kind": "succeed", "name": "done", "output": { "kind": "null" }, "bindings": [] }
    }
  ],
  "otherwise": {
    "kind": "fail",
    "name": "review_attempts_exhausted",
    "reason": "review_attempts_exhausted"
  }
}

docs.title: 5. The complete graph
6. Bind the agents
docs.text:
The runtime plan has one binding per executable node, keyed by node name: worker, acceptance, and code.

review-loop.runtime.json
{
  "harness": "codex",
  "provider": "openai",
  "size": "medium",
  "nodes": {
    "worker": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "model": "YOUR_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "node_instance"
    },
    "acceptance": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "model": "YOUR_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "execution"
    },
    "code": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "model": "YOUR_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "execution"
    }
  }
}

The worker uses node_instance, so each loop pass continues the same provider conversation. The reviewers use execution, so each review starts a fresh session and does not see the previous pass. The graph state still carries the feedback explicitly either way.

Replace YOUR_MODEL_ID with a model the provider accepts. Nodes can use different models, effort values, or harnesses and providers; size applies to the whole run. The bindings omit connections, so a local Codex run reuses the Codex CLI's login, and a Docker or Platform target derives the canonical OPENAI_API_KEY requirement. See the RuntimePlan reference for every field.

docs.title: 7. Validate, then run
docs.text:
The input supplies only the task:

input.json
{
  "task": "Add a health-check endpoint that returns HTTP 200. Add focused tests and keep the change scoped."
}

From the folder you want to change (or with --cwd FOLDER), check all three files without starting a run. Validation covers JSON shape, graph data flow, loop termination, runtime coverage, and the initial input:

zeroshot run \
  --title "Review loop validation" \
  --graph ~/review-loop/review-loop.graph.json \
  --runtime-config ~/review-loop/review-loop.runtime.json \
  --input ~/review-loop/input.json \
  --validate-only

Successful validation writes {"valid":true}.

Remove --validate-only to start the run:

zeroshot run \
  --title "Health-check endpoint" \
  --graph ~/review-loop/review-loop.graph.json \
  --runtime-config ~/review-loop/review-loop.runtime.json \
  --input ~/review-loop/input.json

Observe and control runs covers status, logs, and stopping.

The same files run on a target with --target platform (see Connect Zeroshot Platform) or the name of a direct target. A target requires an exact Git source selected from the checkout or source overrides, and resolves OPENAI_API_KEY from the submission environment or its connection store. The graph has no delivery node, so a target run does not push the accepted change. Add a Git delivery verifier after the loop, or use the software-change template, which defaults to a PR. Choose --push for branch publication or --ship for merge delivery.

docs.title: Cross-vendor review
docs.text:
A reviewer from the worker's model family can share its blind spots. An agent binding can carry its own lane, a harness and provider pair that overrides the plan's default. This runtime plan keeps the worker on Codex and runs both reviewers on Claude Code; the graph does not change:

review-loop.cross-vendor.runtime.json
{
  "harness": "codex",
  "provider": "openai",
  "size": "medium",
  "nodes": {
    "worker": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "model": "YOUR_OPENAI_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "node_instance"
    },
    "acceptance": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "lane": {
        "harness": "claude",
        "provider": "anthropic"
      },
      "model": "YOUR_ANTHROPIC_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "execution"
    },
    "code": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "lane": {
        "harness": "claude",
        "provider": "anthropic"
      },
      "model": "YOUR_ANTHROPIC_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "execution"
    }
  }
}

Replace YOUR_OPENAI_MODEL_ID with a model OpenAI accepts and YOUR_ANTHROPIC_MODEL_ID with one Anthropic accepts. Pass the file to --runtime-config in step 7 in place of review-loop.runtime.json.

A local run needs both the Codex CLI and Claude Code installed and signed in. Before the run starts, Zeroshot checks that codex and claude are on PATH; it does not check login state, so a missing Claude Code login fails at the first review. On a target, the run requires both OPENAI_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and the target must advertise openengine.node-runtime-lanes/v1. The CLI refuses to send the plan to a target that does not.

docs.title: Review a pull request
docs.text: The pr-review template checks a PR's implementation and posts a concise Markdown comment. PR review uses comment delivery so comparison preparation always has an admitted publisher. The separate issue-review template retains a basic issue-proposal review; its review workflow will be designed separately.

docs.title: What the graph checks
docs.text:
The classifier inspects the captured diff and linked requirements. It requests one reproduction for a fix, feature, UI change, or material correctness, security, persistence, or integration risk. It skips reproduction only for clearly small, uncritical changes such as documentation or a mechanical refactor. Missing tools or services cannot justify skipping a required check.

When requested, the reproducer exercises the changed workflow through the full local stack. UI changes require browser checks. It records command and browser results, including failed checks and environment blockers, without repairing reviewed code. A missing prerequisite remains an explicit verification gap.

The code checker then inspects the diff and its callers for correctness, lean implementation, and clean abstraction boundaries. It checks full coverage of linked issue acceptance criteria unless the PR or caller explicitly declares partial scope, and incorporates the reproduction evidence into the final comment. The comment has a 150-word instruction budget: actionable findings, a brief Reproduction: sentence naming the stack/browser, user action and observed result, and a Setup: sentence reporting startup problems and workarounds, including resolved ones. A skipped reproduction gives its reason. Detailed evidence stays in run history or artifacts. The native header records the captured revisions once.

The native publisher posts the report after these agents settle. A successful run confirms completion and publication; findings or blocked tests can still appear in its report.

docs.title: Prepare the runtime and credentials
docs.text:
The supplied runtime plan assigns all three agents gpt-6.1-sol at xhigh on Codex/OpenAI with independent execution sessions. Save it as runtime.json and pass it through --runtime-config. The publisher is native and has no model. Model choices remain in the caller's runtime plan rather than the graph.

Comment delivery uses the github connection's GH_TOKEN, as other GitHub delivery does. Provide that field through a named connection or the invoking environment. For a local run using a stored GitHub CLI login, resolve GH_TOKEN from gh auth token before submission. Publication credentials belong to the native node and are not declared on the review agents.

Local metadata resolution accepts GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or a native GitHub CLI login. Named targets resolve metadata through their task-resolution route. Hosted targets use host-owned credentials; direct targets require GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN in the invoking environment. Targets must advertise task resolution and comment delivery; an older target refuses before submission.

docs.title: Run the review
docs.text:
Select a clean checkout already at the PR head. Zeroshot refuses a mismatch instead of switching or resetting the worktree.

zeroshot run --title "Review PR 123" \
  --template pr-review \
  --task-from https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY/pull/123 \
  --runtime-config runtime.json \
  --cwd /path/to/pr-checkout \
  --submission-key review-pr-123

For hosted execution, add --target platform and select a repository environment that prepares the required stack and browser tools. Source comes from URL resolution, so a client checkout is unnecessary. A saved PR review profile already contains its runtime and publisher; use --profile org:pr-review without template or delivery overrides.

--validate-only prepares and validates without executing agents. Ordinary --input FILE passes JSON unchanged and is mutually exclusive with --task-from.

docs.title: Input and result
docs.text:
Fetching happens before the graph starts. PR intake captures {url, context} with title/body, complete context.reviewScope base/head identities, and required context.linkedIssues. Linked issue entries contain {url, title, body} from GitHub's manual or keyword-based closing relationships. Plain mentions do not create that relationship; the checker must report referenced requirements as unverified if their issue text is absent. An empty array means the selected GitHub identity exposed no linked closing issues. Incomplete or erroring metadata refuses preparation; intake never silently truncates issues. The bounded snapshot supports up to 100 linked issues. See GitHub's linking rules.

There is no mandatory task field. Optional caller instructions can narrow review focus or declare partial implementation. PR comparison uses the admitted head against its merge base with the captured base revision, including fork heads; publication refuses a changed review scope. The graph accepts PR context; select issue-review with an issue URL for the separate basic path.

The result contains a receipt with the comment permalink, identity, and body hash. Comment publication never commits or pushes the review workspace. A custom graph can supply {url, body} directly without an agent or local repository.

Retry uncertain submission with the same explicit submission key and authored configuration. The CLI retains prepared input/source, so retries do not silently read newer discussion text. Resume uses admitted input. One immutable comment belongs to each delivery lineage: matching retries reuse it, while changed report content refuses with its URL. An uncertain POST reconciles remote evidence and fails explicitly if unconfirmed; it never authorizes a blind repost.

docs.title: Prepare a runtime environment
docs.text:
Run submissions to Docker targets accept an environment field alongside runtime:

{
  "environment": {
    "setup": "apt-get update && apt-get install -y jq",
    "startup": "npm ci",
    "variables": { "CI": "true" }
  }
}

Profiles contain graph and agent settings and have no environment reference. Supply the concrete definition when submitting a run. With the CLI, put the contents of environment above into a JSON file and pass --environment FILE alongside your profile. --no-environment sends an explicit empty definition ({}), which bypasses defaults on hosts that provide them. Omitting both flags leaves selection to the host. Direct Docker uses the base environment when none is supplied. Merge-plan manifests also accept a top-level environment; the definition applies to each run in that plan, while omission allows the host to resolve each repository's default.

Hosts may provide saved environments and choose repository defaults before accepting a run. Zeroshot executes the resolved definition and preserves it for queued and resumed attempts; it does not store environment resources or interpret repository defaults. The local UI has no environment catalog or selector. Connection values come from the existing target connection mechanism and never belong in scripts or public variables. Only explicitly declared hook connections reach preparation; node connections remain independently declared. If installation needs private registry access, add "connections": { "package-registry": ["NPM_TOKEN"] } to the definition. The CLI can collect hook credentials for a definition you supply. When a host selects a default, its connection store must supply those credentials; the CLI does not inspect saved environments to discover additional secrets in your shell.

docs.title: Example: pinned Node and npm dependencies
docs.text:
For a repository with a committed package-lock.json, save this as setup.sh. It installs OS packages and Node 22.22.3, verifies the archive against the release's SHA-256 checksums, and exposes Node to every agent through $ZEROSHOT_TOOLS/bin:

set -euo pipefail
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
apt-get update -qq
apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends jq sqlite3 xz-utils

case "$(uname -m)" in
  x86_64) arch=x64 ;;
  aarch64) arch=arm64 ;;
  *) echo 'Unsupported Node architecture' >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
version=22.22.3
release="node-v$version-linux-$arch"
download=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$download"' EXIT
curl -fsSL "https://nodejs.org/dist/v$version/$release.tar.xz" -o "$download/$release.tar.xz"
curl -fsSL "https://nodejs.org/dist/v$version/SHASUMS256.txt" -o "$download/SHASUMS256.txt"
(cd "$download" && sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHASUMS256.txt)
tar -xJf "$download/$release.tar.xz" -C "$ZEROSHOT_TOOLS"
for tool in node npm npx; do
  ln -sfn "../$release/bin/$tool" "$ZEROSHOT_TOOLS/bin/$tool"
done
node --version

Save the workspace preparation as startup.sh. npm ci rebuilds node_modules from the lockfile, so this also works after restoring a workspace:

set -euo pipefail
test "$(node --version)" = v22.22.3
npm ci --no-audit --no-fund

On your machine, use jq to embed both scripts in a flat environment file, then submit it with your existing profile, task input file, and target:

jq -n --rawfile setup setup.sh --rawfile startup startup.sh \
  '{setup: $setup, startup: $startup, variables: {CI: "true"}}' > environment.json
zeroshot run --profile my-profile --target my-target \
  --environment environment.json --title "Fix the failing test" --input input.json

The file contains setup and startup directly; an inline run API request puts the same object in submission.environment, beside submission.runtime. Setup cannot read repository files because checkout has not happened yet. Startup can invoke a checked-in script, for example bash .zeroshot/startup.sh.

docs.title: Lifecycle and installation conventions
docs.text:
Submission returns after admission and durable acceptance. While the run is admitted, setup runs as root before source checkout or workspace restoration. Startup then runs as the workspace user, with the checkout as its current directory. The graph starts only after both succeed. Watch run logs for phase progress and command output. Nonzero exits become environment_setup_failed or environment_startup_failed; a preparation deadline becomes environment_preparation_timeout. These stop the run without using any graph repair attempts. Force-stop works during preparation and waits for process cleanup before recording its terminal result.

Each hook uses Bash with errexit and pipefail and has fifteen minutes, inside one thirty-minute preparation budget. Install OS packages in setup. Install shared executable tools under $ZEROSHOT_TOOLS/bin, which is on the PATH of every hook and agent, and project dependencies in the workspace. Shell exports affect only that hook; use variables for later commands. The platform's harness Node interpreter remains separate from a project-installed Node version. Setup, startup, and agent sessions have separate home directories; use $ZEROSHOT_TOOLS for tools shared across them.

Workers and reviewers share files, ignored dependencies, generated output, and services. Startup can start a background service; its process belongs to the run and survives individual agent executions. Wait for required services to be ready before startup exits; the runtime does not infer their health. Setup is for installation: start services from startup. Do not daemonize processes or start root services in setup. Setup cancellation cleans up its shell process group; a root script can escape that group, so this is not containment for untrusted root code. The target images suppress Debian package service autostart. Parallel graph branches share mutable state, so scripts and graphs must coordinate concurrent writes.

Both hooks run again on resume: setup, restore workspace files, startup, then restart or continue the graph. Startup must be idempotent with respect to existing workspace files. Checkpoints do not restore running services, Docker images or volumes, database transactions, or agent conversations. A background process may change files while a checkpoint is captured; use application-managed exports for consistent database recovery.

A direct Docker target is an operator-trusted container. Root setup changes that container's OS, including for other runs it hosts. Use separate disposable target containers for independent OS requirements. The target must have a writable root for package installation. Docker commands need an operator-provided daemon endpoint. Detached Docker containers belong to that daemon and are not terminated by the target's process cleanup. Direct target operators or scripts must manage their names, reuse, and removal. When the daemon runs inside a disposable run machine, destroying that machine removes its Docker resources. Local execution uses the invoking machine and rejects setup and startup hooks and their connection references.

docs.title: Source-code adapters
docs.text:
Local folders, Git transport, and forge delivery are separate concerns. A local graph without delivery needs no source identity. Contained runs require an exact Git source. The existing push, PR, and merge nodes keep their receipt, repair, cancellation, and recovery behavior across providers.

Operation Required implementation Checkout and push over HTTPS or SSH Shared Git transport Review creation, checks, feedback, and merge Registered forge adapter

GitLab, Forgejo, and other Git hosts can use checkout and push now. Their forge APIs need adapters for PR and merge behavior. GitHub is the maintained forge implementation.

docs.title: Ownership and registration
docs.text:
zeroshot/src/source_code/provider/ contains effect-free contracts and SourceCodeProviderRegistry. Provider, repository, and review identities are bounded opaque values; GitHub grammar and policy belong to its implementation.

Maintained implementations live in zeroshot/src/source_code/adapters/core/. Contributions live in zeroshot/src/source_code/adapters/contributed/ and register through that folder's register hook. The same registry proves required capabilities during preflight and returns delivery authority during composition. Metadata-only registration must perform no filesystem, process, credential, or network effects. The provider's pure repository_from_remote hook identifies its forge from a credential-free Git locator text after the run boundary validates the URL. Contracts stay independent of protocol and process implementations. The same registry rejects ambiguous matches; both local and named CLI source selection use it. Runtime registration receives the selected source and scoped shared Git transport.

Implement SourceCodeProvider for descriptor and source operations, and SourceDeliveryAuthority for the existing delivery workflow. A forge owns its credential field, repository and review grammar, checks, policy, and authoritative merge result. Git effects reuse the shared transport. A custom API token never acquires GitHub Git authentication authority. Provider credentials are available only through the admitted delivery connection or private source capability.

Adding a forge needs no new delivery node family or closed forge enum. Embedders can register adapters in SourceCodeProviderRegistry and use registry-aware admission. The contribution acceptance test admits an opaque nested repository and review ID, uses its own token field and credential refresh, and drives the existing PR and merge nodes through the supervisor and ledger.

docs.title: Required behavior
docs.text:
An adapter must observe remote identity before effects, preserve the reviewed candidate SHA and published ancestry, and reconcile confirmed success after a lost response. It must distinguish transport errors, authentication refusal, provider policy/schema errors, and candidate repair. Review creation may allocate a new opaque ID. Merge receipts record the observed integrated revision; requests cannot predict it.

Source credential values stay out of source records, receipts, profiles, and history. Shared transport owns bounded capture, redaction, private SSH files, cancellation, and process cleanup. Recovery preserves the original delivery branch and review identity while obtaining fresh authorized values.

Run the shared provider contract tests and existing delivery tests, plus the contributed adapter's own tests. Include unknown/unsupported capabilities, opaque identities, credential rotation, lost responses, remote branch movement, cancellation, and failed cleanup.

The production registration hook is compiled into the maintained local and hosted factories. An embedder may provide its own registry to admission and use that registry's delivery authority when composing a candidate or allocator. Built-in placements use the contributed registration hook.

The registry's coordinated delivery workflow obtains a scoped adapter through SourceCodeProvider.delivery_authority. Its descriptor advertises the operations that adapter supports. The older inspect_operation/operate contract remains available for callers of atomic operations; maintained adapters currently return an explicit unavailable error through that seam. Forge credential selection has one authority: SourceDeliveryAuthority.forge_credential_field.

Conversation comments are a separate operation exposed through the same registry's optional comment authority. Pure URL identification and capability admission do not require a Git source. The native publisher owns bounded create/reconciliation and a durable lineage publication store; the forge supplies actor, comment identity, paginated reads, creation, and exact review-scope checks. Comment authority does not acquire Git transport access or a model session.

docs.title: Documentation versions
docs.text:
Current follows main and is the default. It may describe changes that have not shipped yet. For an installed release, choose its minor version from the header. Each minor version documents its newest published patch: releases 10.2.0 through 10.2.8 share v10.2/, whose content comes from 10.2.8 after that release publishes.

Patch releases update the existing minor documentation without adding another selector entry. Older minor versions remain available.

docs.title: URL contract
docs.text:
The docs base is https://zeroshot.sh/docs/, which serves the GitHub Pages site at https://the-open-engine.github.io/zeroshot/. Resolve these paths against either base:

Relative path Meaning current/ Current main documentation; the site root redirects here vX.Y/ Newest published patch within that minor version versions.json Selector entries: Current and minor versions current/manifest.json, vX.Y/manifest.json Source identity and logical routes dev/ Legacy page redirects to Current stable/ Legacy page redirects to the newest released minor vX.Y.Z/ Previously published patch pages redirect to their minor version

The selector does not list legacy aliases. Existing patch links retain their page, query string, and fragment, but now show the minor version's newest patch. New releases do not create patch paths.

Search engines should index Current. A minor version's page declares the same page in Current as its canonical URL, or its own https://zeroshot.sh/docs/vX.Y/ URL when Current no longer has that page. The publisher reapplies this to every minor version on each publication.

docs.title: Build manifest
docs.text:
Manifest schema 2 distinguishes a docs channel from the exact product used to generate its APIs:

{
  "schemaVersion": 2,
  "docsVersion": "v10.2",
  "productVersion": "10.2.8",
  "pythonSdkVersion": "10.2.8.post1",
  "sourceCommit": "FULL_PRODUCT_SOURCE_COMMIT",
  "publisherCommit": "FULL_PUBLICATION_WORKFLOW_COMMIT",
  "routes": {
    "overview": "",
    "runtimePlan": "concepts/runtimes-and-connections/",
    "runControl": "guides/observe-and-control/",
    "cli": "zeroshot-cli/",
    "pythonApi": "reference/python/",
    "clusterApi": "reference/cluster/api/"
  }
}

The example abbreviates routes; builds list every logical route their source documents, including protocol schemas. Values are relative to the selected version root. Current uses docsVersion: current and null product and Python SDK versions; its source commit identifies main at build time.

A minor's manifest lists only routes its source documents; clients must treat a missing route key as not documented in that version.

Publication tools and this version-policy page can come from a newer workflow commit than the product source. publisherCommit records that distinction. Minor pages migrated from the old site retain their original source identity and omit publisherCommit until rebuilt; their existing rendered product content is reused.

Old patch manifests now contain a schema-2 redirect record such as {"schemaVersion": 2, "redirect": "../v10.2/manifest.json"}. This is JSON metadata, not an HTTP redirect: GitHub Pages cannot redirect JSON clients with its HTML redirect pages. Clients that need an exact historical patch manifest must use the site's Git history. Do not treat a minor manifest as proof that the docs match an older patch exactly.

docs.title: Linking from Zeroshot Platform
docs.text:
For a deployed product version X.Y.Z, fetch vX.Y/manifest.json and require schema 2. Confirm that productVersion belongs to the deployed major/minor line, then resolve a logical route against vX.Y/. For example, 10.2.3 uses the v10.2 docs, whose manifest may identify 10.2.8. Callers should label this as minor-version documentation and account for features added after their installed patch. Compare source commits only when the documented and deployed product versions match.

If the minor has no docs, offer an explicitly labelled Current link. Current may contain unreleased behavior. Platform owns instructions for accounts, organization policy, OAuth, GitHub Apps, and capacity; core graph, runtime, CLI, protocol, and SDK material stays here.

docs.title: Publication and recovery
docs.text:
Every main publication updates Current. After Python SDK revision 1, a product release updates its minor documentation from the exact release tag and commit. A retry cannot replace a newer patch with an older one or substitute a different source for the same product version. Later Python-only revisions do not rebuild product docs.

To retry, run Publish versioned documentation. Omit inputs for Current, or supply the exact vX.Y.Z release and source commit for a minor. The optional stable input maintains the legacy released-docs redirect; it never changes the site's Current default.

The publisher consolidates existing patch snapshots before publishing, retaining the newest patch per minor and replacing old pages with redirects. It stages the complete result before pushing gh-pages and deploying through GitHub Pages Actions. No release tags or binary artifacts change. If a release is the first publication, the publisher first builds Current from main in an isolated checkout, then publishes the requested minor from its release source. Both become visible together.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
The public package is zeroshot; the install distribution is the-open-engine-zeroshot. All I/O methods are asynchronous. Public data objects are frozen dataclasses, and exact protocol documents are copied defensively at their boundary.

The reference is generated from the curated exports in zeroshot.__init__ and their source docstrings:

  • Client and run handle: run and merge-plan submission, lookup, observation, and stop operations.
  • Configuration: targets, run requests, merge-plan DAGs, and runtimes.
  • Result models: immutable run, plan, log, source, and terminal values.
  • Exceptions: request, target, protocol, timeout, and failed-run errors.

See the Python SDK guide for complete submissions and target examples.

docs.title: Version identity
docs.text: The SDK release paired with Zeroshot vX.Y.Z is X.Y.Z.post1. This site records that value in its version manifest. If a later SDK-only revision is published, it does not alter an existing core docs snapshot.

docs.title: RuntimePlan
docs.text:
A RuntimePlan says how each executable node in a graph runs. It selects the run size and a default harness and provider, and gives every step and verifier one binding. It contains model identifiers and connection field names, never secret values.

Runtimes and connections explains the concepts, and Build a review loop builds a complete plan for a custom graph. The Rust types in openengine-cluster-protocol are authoritative; the generated protocol schema is the machine-readable contract.

docs.title: Document fields
docs.text:
RuntimePlan is a closed JSON object. The following four fields are required; unknown fields are rejected.

Field Value harness Harness of the default lane: codex, claude, copilot, or pi provider Provider of the default lane, supported by the selected harness size small, medium, or large nodes Object mapping each executable graph node name to a node binding

Optional activeMemory controls repository and graph recall/collection independently, and globalAgents.postmortem configures the built-in after-run specialists. Both default to enabled on local CLI runs and direct targets. The same sections are accepted by uniform runtime files. See Active Memory for budgets, provider inheritance and opt-out examples.

harness and provider form the default lane. Every agent node runs on it unless its binding carries its own lane. size applies to the whole run. Model, effort, session scope, and connections are chosen per node.

size is a run-level resource class. Zeroshot records it with the run and reports it in run status; the hosting target decides what resources each class receives.

nodes keys are graph node names: 1 to 128 bytes matching [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*.

This plan binds the three agent nodes of the built-in software-change template:

{
  "harness": "claude",
  "provider": "anthropic",
  "size": "medium",
  "nodes": {
    "worker": { "kind": "agent", "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID", "sessionScope": "node_instance" },
    "acceptance": { "kind": "agent", "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID", "effort": "high" },
    "code": { "kind": "agent", "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID", "effort": "high" }
  }
}

docs.title: Harness and provider
docs.text:
harness selects which provider values parse:

harness provider codex openai, openrouter, bedrock, gateway claude anthropic, openrouter, bedrock, gateway copilot github pi anthropic, openai, openrouter, bedrock, gateway

The same pairs apply to an agent node's lane. Any other pair is rejected when the plan is read.

pi/anthropic and pi/openai reuse a local Pi login from ~/.pi/agent; the other pi lanes need a connection.

pi/gateway carries GATEWAY_BASE_URL, GATEWAY_API_KEY, and GATEWAY_API. The last names the wire protocol as openai-responses, openai-completions, or anthropic-messages, so one lane reaches any endpoint Pi implements and the model identifier stays opaque and caller-owned. Zeroshot never infers the protocol from the identifier, and an unrecognized value fails before launch.

To send the anthropic lane to a caller-owned Messages-compatible endpoint, declare ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL with any one of the lane's credentials (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, or ANTHROPIC_OAUTH_TOKEN); a local run also honors the invoking shell's ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. The endpoint override interpolates the API key only when the connection supplies it, so a token keeps Pi's own environment authentication. The openai lane likewise honors OPENAI_BASE_URL or OPENAI_API_BASE. Pi ignores these variables itself, so Zeroshot turns each into a provider override that keeps that provider's own protocol; the openai lane therefore needs a Responses-compatible endpoint, and any other protocol uses pi/gateway. A declared endpoint ends native-login reuse, so the stored login is never sent to that host.

Pi has no permission control of its own, so a contained pi run relies on the disposable capsule rather than a bypass argument.

docs.title: Node bindings
docs.text: kind selects an agent, Git delivery, or comment delivery binding. Fields belonging to another kind are rejected.

docs.title: agent
docs.text:
Field Required Value kind Yes agent lane No Harness and provider; default lane when omitted model Yes Provider-owned model identifier, 1 to 2,048 non-control characters effort No low, medium, high, xhigh, or max; unset when omitted sessionScope No execution (default) or node_instance connections No Connection declarations; empty when omitted

Zeroshot passes model and effort to the harness unchanged. It keeps no model catalog and does not check whether a model supports the chosen effort.

sessionScope controls provider conversation state. It does not change graph state or bindings.

sessionScope Behavior execution Opens a fresh provider session for each execution of the node, then closes it node_instance Reuses one session when the same node instance runs again, for example across loop iterations

If a reused session is lost, Zeroshot fails that execution with session_lost. It does not open a replacement session silently.

docs.title: git_delivery
docs.text:
Field Required Value kind Yes git_delivery connections No Connection declarations; empty when omitted pullRequestFeedback No consider (default) or ignore

A git_delivery binding has no model, effort, session scope, or lane. Admission accepts it only on a verifier node whose worker is one of the built-in delivery workers:

Worker Accepts pullRequestFeedback: ignore builtin.git-delivery.push@1 No builtin.git-delivery.pr@1 No builtin.git-delivery.pr@2 Yes builtin.git-delivery.merge@1 No builtin.git-delivery.merge@2 No builtin.git-delivery.merge@3 Yes

The delivery verifier cannot have authored instructions, must use attempts: 1, and must declare the output, signals, and diagnostic of its worker's fixed contract. zeroshot template show software-change --pr prints a delivery node with the current contract.

A graph can contain at most one delivery node, and no other executable node may run in parallel with it, either as a par sibling or inside a map that can have more than one item. A hosting service may require exactly one delivery node; Zeroshot Platform quick runs require one. See concurrent workspace changes.

ignore skips pull-request discussion. CI, conflict, freshness, and merge-policy checks still apply.

docs.title: comment_delivery
docs.text:
This binding accepts only kind: "comment_delivery" and optional connections. It has no model, lane, effort, or provider session. It binds a verifier using builtin.comment-delivery.post@1 with that worker's fixed input/output, signal, and diagnostic contracts and no authored instructions.

The node reads a required discussion url and report body, plus optional captured reviewScope. Its URL and present scope bind directly from required caller input; they cannot change before publication. A graph permits one trusted delivery node, and comment publication must follow all other executable work and cleanup, outside loops and maps. The exact confirmed receipt must appear in terminal output. See Review an issue or pull request.

docs.title: Per-node lanes
docs.text:
A lane is one harness and provider pair. The plan's harness and provider are the default lane for every agent node, and an agent binding can carry its own lane. A node's effective lane is its lane, or the default lane when it has none. size stays run-level.

This plan binds the same three nodes as the first example. worker runs on the default codex/openai lane, and both reviewers run on Claude Code:

{
  "harness": "codex",
  "provider": "openai",
  "size": "medium",
  "nodes": {
    "worker": { "kind": "agent", "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID", "sessionScope": "node_instance" },
    "acceptance": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "lane": { "harness": "claude", "provider": "anthropic" },
      "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID",
      "effort": "high"
    },
    "code": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "lane": { "harness": "claude", "provider": "anthropic" },
      "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID",
      "effort": "high"
    }
  }
}

Each model goes to the provider of its node's effective lane, so here worker needs an OpenAI model identifier and the reviewers need Anthropic ones.

  • lane accepts the same pairs as the run level, listed in Harness and provider. An invalid pair is rejected when the plan is read.
  • A git_delivery or comment_delivery binding cannot carry a lane.
  • A lane equal to the run-level pair is accepted, and the node runs exactly as it would without one. It is still a lane field, so the target support check applies to it and older binaries reject it. Omit lane when a node should use the default lane.

Zeroshot starts one harness adapter for each distinct effective lane, and each node runs on its own lane's CLI. Model, effort, session scope, and connections stay per node. Provider access defaults also come from each node's effective lane; see Connections.

docs.title: Target support
docs.text:
Targets that support lanes advertise openengine.node-runtime-lanes/v1 in their discovery document. Before the CLI submits a run or stores a profile on a target, it checks the plan. If any node carries a lane and the target does not advertise the capability, the command fails after reading the target's discovery document and before it requests an access token or sends the plan:

target operation failed: target does not support per-node runtime lanes (openengine.node-runtime-lanes/v1)

Plans without a lane are unchanged on the wire and work with every target. Older Zeroshot binaries reject a plan that contains a lane field when they read it.

Local profiles are saved together in one file in the configuration store (ZEROSHOT_CONFIG_DIR). Once any local profile carries a lane, an older binary cannot read that file at all. Every local profile command, --profile local:NAME run, and zeroshot acp session then fails, including for profiles without lanes:

local controller operation failed: local profile store is malformed

To run an older binary beside a newer one, give it its own ZEROSHOT_CONFIG_DIR. To recover, remove the profile or its lane fields with the newer binary.

docs.title: Local runs
docs.text:
Before the controller starts, a local zeroshot run or zeroshot resume checks that each lane's executable, codex, claude, copilot, or pi, is on PATH. A missing executable fails the command with a message such as:

lane claude/anthropic needs the `claude` executable on PATH

zeroshot acp runs the same check when each session opens, against that session's workspace, and the session request fails with the same message. When every PATH entry is absolute, it also checks at startup. An empty or relative entry resolves against the directory the harness starts in, which is known only per session, so then the startup check is skipped. The check does not inspect login state; a missing login surfaces at that lane's first turn. As in a single-lane run, local codex/openai, claude/anthropic, copilot/github, pi/anthropic, and pi/openai lanes reuse their harness's native login, and other lanes need their provider's connection fields; see Connections.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
nodes contains exactly one binding for every step and verifier in the graph, keyed by the node name. Structural nodes (seq, choice, par, loop, map) and terminal nodes (succeed, fail) never get a binding. Admission rejects:

  • a missing binding for an executable node;
  • a binding for a structural, terminal, or unknown node;
  • a git_delivery binding on a step, or on a verifier that does not use a delivery worker;
  • an agent binding on a node that uses a delivery worker;
  • an agent binding on a node without authored instructions;
  • a worker reference reused on several nodes with a different contract or binding kind.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
connections maps a connection key to the exact environment field names the node may receive. Values come from the submission environment or a target connection store at run time.

The example below is the shape a Pi gateway lane uses: GATEWAY_API names its wire protocol and is Pi-specific. Other lanes list only their own provider's fields.

{
  "connections": {
    "gateway": ["GATEWAY_BASE_URL", "GATEWAY_API_KEY", "GATEWAY_API"]
  }
}
Item Limit Connection key 1 to 128 bytes, no control characters Field name [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*, at most 128 bytes Field list At least one name, no duplicates Keys per node At most 64 Field names per node At most 64, and one name cannot appear under two keys in the same node Unique field names per run At most 64 across all nodes

The per-run limit also counts the connection fields and variable names of an attached runtime environment. Each connection value must be 1 byte to 64 KiB with no NUL. The static connection values supplied for one run, counting each key and field name with its value, must fit in 256 KiB.

When a node omits connections, Zeroshot derives provider access from that node's effective lane for the execution placement. Local native logins need no declaration; contained targets and non-native providers receive the canonical requirements listed in Runtimes and connections. A run's connection requirements are the union over its nodes, so a plan that mixes lanes can require the fields of several providers.

docs.title: Uniform runtime configuration
docs.text:
--uniform-runtime-config accepts a single agent configuration and expands it into a full plan:

Field Required Value harness Yes As in RuntimePlan provider Yes As in RuntimePlan size No As in RuntimePlan; default medium model Yes As in an agent binding effort No As in an agent binding sessionScope No As in an agent binding connections No Applied to every agent node

Every executable node gets an agent binding with these values, except nodes that use a delivery worker. Those get a git_delivery binding as described below.

When selecting the built-in software-change template, omitted sessionScope defaults to node_instance for worker and execution for its reviewers. The worker retains its session through implementation and every repair; reviewers start fresh each pass. An explicit uniform sessionScope still applies to every agent. Exact runtime plans and saved graphs retain their authored scopes; use node_instance on worker in an exact plan to retain its session. When using the updated template with an older exact runtime config, remove its review_repair and delivery_repair bindings. Existing saved profiles keep their stored graph and bindings.

For auto-research, an omitted uniform sessionScope defaults to node_instance for explorer, synthesizer, challenger, and researcher, and execution for reviewer. The normal round has these five agent bindings; --push adds checkpoint_delivery. Exact plans must supply these node names and their desired scopes. Existing saved profiles keep their stored topology and runtime.

A uniform configuration applies one lane to every agent node. Neither --uniform-runtime-config nor the Python SDK's UniformRuntime can express per-node lanes; use an exact --runtime-config or an opaque RuntimePlan instead.

docs.title: Template delivery bindings
docs.text:
Built-in templates own their delivery nodes. software-change defaults to a pull-request delivery verifier named deliver; --push and --ship select push and merge delivery, and --delivery none omits delivery. The existing worker handles delivery repairs. With auto-research, --push adds only the trusted checkpoint_delivery node; the researcher and reviewer already handle the round records and delivery description. single-worker has no delivery modes.

The CLI inserts a git_delivery binding with no forge connection for push, or {"github": ["GH_TOKEN"]} for PR and merge. Git transport uses the selected source credentials. --no-pr-feedback (requires pull-request or merge delivery) sets pullRequestFeedback to ignore.

A uniform configuration binds the added agent nodes too. An exact --runtime-config must bind all agent nodes itself. Software-change uses worker, acceptance, and code with every delivery mode. It may omit the delivery node; if it includes it, the binding must be git_delivery. List the executable nodes with zeroshot template show TEMPLATE plus the same delivery flag.

Custom graphs author delivery in both the graph and the plan.

docs.title: Admission
docs.text: This document defines the stateful plan, apply, and get admission contract. The Rust wire types are authoritative. Admission accepts only GraphSpec; it does not execute graph nodes.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
plan({graph}) invokes the configured verifier and returns {ok, diagnostics, bounds?}. bounds is present only after approval. Planning is pure in the graph: it never reads cluster state or an idempotency record and never writes the control journal or verified-I/O ledger.

apply({graph, input?, dryRun?, ifGeneration?, idempotencyKey?}) defaults dryRun to false.

  • Dry run omits input and idempotencyKey, verifies the graph, and returns a deterministic node diff against the committed compiled IR. It creates no generation, run, cursor, journal entry, seed entry, or idempotency record.
  • Committed apply requires a non-empty idempotency key of at most 256 non-control characters.
  • A create or changed compiled identity requires input, validates it against the graph's closed initialInput payload type, assigns a new run ID, and commits generation 1 or the next JavaScript-safe generation.
  • An unchanged compiled identity omits input, preserves generation and run ID, and records only the idempotency receipt. Supplying a new root input for an unchanged graph is resubmit's job, not apply's; see lifecycle.md.

get({atCursor?}) returns the committed GraphSpec, status, and cursor from one atomic aggregate snapshot. The logical control journal and verified-I/O seed ledger must identify the same current run and cursor. An empty snapshot has no spec, compiled IR, generation, run, cursor, or seed. A running or finished snapshot has all six, uses a positive generation, and has a seed matching its run and admission cursor. Its operational lifecycle snapshot has a matching durable latest cursor and metadata; lifecycle events advance that cursor without changing the admission cursor. Transient admitting preserves either the complete prior committed snapshot or the complete empty snapshot; it never exposes partially staged state. initialize and get fail closed when a store violates these invariants.
